dimension: Peer-to-peer coordination with no central server, and reputation among untrusted peers
summary:
The founder's instinct is sound and the field is 25 years old. Three results bear hardest on CDSFL.

First, optimistic unchoking already IS the cold-start mechanism he is reaching for. BitTorrent's choke algorithm re-ranks partners every 10 seconds by measured download rate from them, and every third round (about 30 seconds) gives 1 slot to a randomly chosen interested peer regardless of history (Cohen, "Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent", P2PECON 2003; described identically in Legout/Urvoy-Keller/Michiardi, IMC 2006, pp. 203-216). That is explore-versus-exploit with a bounded exploration budget of roughly 25% of slots, run per-peer with no coordinator and no prior. It needs no "capability" concept at all: rate measured against self is the rank.

Second, heterogeneity is handled by emergence, not by design. Legout, Liogkas, Kohler and Zhang instrumented a private torrent of more than 40 nodes and measured that peers cluster with similar-bandwidth peers, and that this clustering disappears when the initial seed is underprovisioned (arXiv cs/0611105). "Don't pitch a desktop against a supercomputer" is what reciprocal rate-matching does by itself.

Third, and this is the hard one: the founder's two hard constraints — capability must be MEASURED, and participants may be arbitrarily heterogeneous — are exactly the two preconditions Douceur names for unbounded identity forgery. His Lemma 1: if rho is the ratio of a faulty entity's resources to a minimally capable entity's, it can present g = rho distinct identities. Admitting a supercomputer and a desktop into one measured ranking sets rho to the hardware ratio and hands that many top-tier slots to whoever owns the big machine. Worse, Douceur section 3.2 shows computation challenges specifically can be batched: given m puzzles an entity finds one witness satisfying all m. A random hard maths problem is a computation challenge.

On the auditable registry: the literature is unambiguous that without a coordinator you get tamper-DETECTION, not tamper-PREVENTION, and detection is conditional on peers comparing views out of band (fork consistency, SUNDR, OSDI 2004). RFC 9162 section 1 concedes this for Certificate Transparency in production and says "it is necessary to treat each log as a trusted third party".
is_the_wheel_already_invented: Mostly yes, and in two separate places. (1) The cold-start mechanism is BitTorrent's optimistic unchoke, published 2003 and running on every torrent client since: a bounded random allocation to an unmeasured peer, rotated every ~30 seconds, which simultaneously bootstraps newcomers and discovers better partners. CDSFL's "hard random maths problem at startup" is a heavier, more attackable version of the same explore-exploit step. (2) The "reassign, never delete; capability is measured, not named" requirement is OurGrid's Network of Favours, published 2004 (Andrade, Brasileiro, Cirne, Mowbray, HPDC 2004), which solves it with an explicit formula: local reputation r_A(B) = max{0, v(B,A) - v(A,B) + sqrt(v(B,A))}. Floored at 0 so a bad performer cannot be worse off than a newcomer (that is the "never set aside" property, and it is also what defeats identity-resetting), and with a SUBLINEAR history term so veterans do not become unovertakeable. Genuinely novel in CDSFL: using the falsification task itself as the capability probe, where verification is asymptotically cheaper than solution (a proof is checkable, a falsifier is runnable). No P2P reputation system in this literature measures capability by having the peer produce its own checkable certificate of competence. That is the one piece worth keeping. What is NOT novel, and what will fail, is making it coordinator-free.

mechanisms.name: BitTorrent choking, tit-for-tat, and optimistic unchoking
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each peer independently ranks interested partners by the data rate it has measured FROM them over the last 10 seconds, unchokes the top 3, and every third round (about 30 seconds) unchokes 1 additional interested peer chosen uniformly at random irrespective of history. No global state, no coordinator, no identity, no reputation record. Optimistic unchoking is explicitly a cold-start exploration mechanism: it bootstraps peers with zero contribution history into the reciprocity game AND discovers better partners than the current top 3. Exploration budget is bounded at roughly 1 of 4 slots.
mechanisms.citation: Bram Cohen, "Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent", 1st Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (P2PECON), Berkeley, 2003. Cadence and rechoke mechanics restated and measured in Arnaud Legout, Guillaume Urvoy-Keller, Pietro Michiardi, "Rarest First and Choke Algorithms Are Enough", ACM IMC 2006, pp. 203-216, DOI 10.1145/1177080.1177106 (arXiv cs/0609026).
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It does not rank from a prior and does not need one. A newcomer has rate 0 and is therefore never in the top 3, but the optimistic unchoke gives it a bounded free sample every 30 seconds; if it reciprocates it enters the measured ranking on its own merit. Cold start is solved by continuous, bounded, random exploration rather than by a startup tournament.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Rank is relative to the measuring peer, not absolute. A slow peer's top 3 are slow peers; a fast peer's top 3 are fast peers. No cross-scale comparison is ever made.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and is strictly better than a startup tournament on three counts. It is continuous (capability drift is tracked, a one-shot startup rank goes stale), it is local (no coordinator computes a global table), and its exploration cost is a fixed fraction of throughput rather than a serial startup phase. What breaks if adopted: there is no global ranking any more. 'Top tier' stops existing as an object; each requester has its own top 3. If CDSFL needs a single auditable statement of record such as 'seat X is tier 1', this mechanism cannot produce one without re-adding an aggregator.

mechanisms.name: Capacity clustering as emergent heterogeneity handling
mechanisms.what_it_does: Reciprocal rate-matching causes peers to self-sort into bandwidth-similar groups without any explicit tiering rule, and the clustering is measurable.
mechanisms.citation: Arnaud Legout, Nikitas Liogkas, Eddie Kohler, Lixia Zhang, "Clustering and Sharing Incentives in BitTorrent Systems", arXiv cs/0611105 (2006); instrumented private torrent, decisions of more than 40 nodes observed. Finds clustering of similar-bandwidth peers AND that an underprovisioned initial seed removes the clustering and weakens sharing incentives.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: No startup phase at all; the clusters form as a side effect of reciprocation.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This IS the answer to 'it does not make sense to pitch a little desktop PC against a vast supercomputer stack'. The stratification is emergent, continuous, and needs no capability estimate.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Directly: pair seats by measured reciprocal usefulness and the tiering falls out. The measured caveat matters more than the result: clustering COLLAPSES when the seed is underprovisioned. For CDSFL the analogue of the seed is the supply of hard, well-posed falsification targets. If targets are scarce relative to roster size, expect the tiering to degenerate and strong seats to subsidise weak ones indiscriminately, exactly as the paper measured.

mechanisms.name: Strategic exploitation of reciprocity (BitTyrant)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Shows that a peer which models its partners' reciprocation thresholds and sends each the minimum that keeps it reciprocating substantially outperforms the honest client, i.e. tit-for-tat as deployed is not incentive-compatible.
mechanisms.citation: Michael Piatek, Tomas Isdal, Thomas Anderson, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Arun Venkataramani, "Do incentives build robustness in BitTorrent?", USENIX NSDI 2007. Measured: median 70% performance gain for a 1 Mb/s strategic client on live swarms; in 114 real swarms with both clients capped at 128 KB/s the median download-time ratio was 1.72 and 25% of strategic downloads finished at least twice as fast. Most of the system's performance was traced to altruistic contribution by high-capacity peers, not to reciprocation. When high-capacity peers behave selfishly, a low-capacity peer's mean completion time rose from 314 to 733 seconds.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start mechanism; it is the falsification of the previous one.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Identifies heterogeneity as the attack surface: the gains accrue specifically to the asymmetry between high- and low-capacity peers.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the falsifier for any CDSFL design that assumes a measured-contribution ranking is self-enforcing. A seat (or its operator) that models the allocator's measurement function can game it at the measured rates above. It transfers with one important mitigation: CDSFL's workload is verifiable in a way file blocks are not (a proof can be checked, a falsifier can be run), so 'minimum that passes' is bounded below by 'actually correct', which BitTorrent has no analogue of. Keep that property; it is the project's real defence.

mechanisms.name: PropShare / proportional-share unchoking
mechanisms.what_it_does: Reframes peer selection as an auction rather than tit-for-tat, shows that under the auction model clients that win receive roughly the same amount regardless of how much they bid, and replaces the fixed-slot allocation with bandwidth shares proportional to what each partner contributed. Proves the proportional-share client strategy-proof within the model.
mechanisms.citation: Dave Levin, Katrina LaCurts, Neil Spring, Bobby Bhattacharjee, "BitTorrent is an Auction: Analyzing and Improving BitTorrent's Incentives", ACM SIGCOMM 2008, pp. 243-254, DOI 10.1145/1402958.1402987.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A contributor with a tiny contribution gets a proportionally tiny but NON-ZERO share, so there is no discrete threshold to clear. This removes the need for a separate newcomer-exception mechanism.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Proportionality is scale-free by construction: a desktop contributing 1% of a seat's intake gets 1% of its output. No tiers, no cutoffs, works identically at any resource ratio.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the single most directly transferable allocation rule in this dimension, and it is a better fit than a knockout bracket. Allocate compute/token budget to each seat in proportion to its measured verified contribution rather than by discrete tier. It satisfies 'no model is ever permanently set aside' automatically (proportional share of a positive total is positive), satisfies 'roster of 1 to 700 without redesign' (no bracket structure to rebuild), and removes the all-or-nothing payoff that makes a tournament worth gaming. What breaks: the notion of a discrete 'top tier' disappears, and CDSFL's existing per-seat configuration that keys off tier labels would need to key off a continuous weight instead.

mechanisms.name: OurGrid Network of Favours (autonomous local reputation, non-negative, sublinear history)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each peer keeps only a LOCAL balance of favours exchanged with each other peer and prioritises high-balance peers under contention. No global reputation, no shared crypto infrastructure, no central authority, and no second-hand testimony, so lying about third parties is structurally impossible. The paper proves a general condition: if collaborators can be identified with sufficient accuracy and get priority, then it pays to be a collaborator, and free riding dies out. Formally, with epsilon(t) the probability a collaborator misdirects a donation to a free rider, v the donor's relative cost, and f(t) the free-rider fraction, collaborating dominates iff epsilon(t) < (1-v)*f(t).
mechanisms.citation: Nazareno Andrade, Francisco Brasileiro, Walfredo Cirne, Miranda Mowbray, "Discouraging Free Riding in a Peer-to-Peer CPU-Sharing Grid", IEEE HPDC 2004 (paper 32). Reputation functions, verbatim from section 3.1: eq. 1 r_A(B) = v(B,A) - v(A,B); eq. 2 r_A(B) = max{0, v(B,A) - v(A,B)}; eq. 3 r_A(B) = max{0, v(B,A) - v(A,B) + log(v(B,A))}; eq. 4 r_A(B) = max{0, v(B,A) - v(A,B) + sqrt(v(B,A))}.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Reputation is defined as exactly 0 for newcomers and is floored at 0 for everyone. A peer that has consumed more than it gave is therefore NOT ranked below a newcomer, which both (a) means no participant is ever excluded and (b) removes the entire gain from resetting identity. The sublinear history term (log or sqrt) is deliberately chosen so the gap between a never-contributor and a small contributor is large, while the gap between two long-standing reciprocators is small, i.e. veterans cannot become unovertakeable.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Balances are in units of donated processing value, local to each pair. A small peer's balances are small in absolute terms but it competes only in each counterparty's own local ordering.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the closest published match to the founder's stated constraints and should be read as the reference design for them. It gives, in one formula, 'measured not named' (balances only, no identity semantics), 'never permanently set aside' (max{0,...}), and whitewash resistance, all without a coordinator. What breaks if adopted: there is no global capability table and no auditable global ranking, because reputation is deliberately subjective and non-transitive. The paper states this as a feature: refusing second-hand evidence is what makes it attack-resistant. If CDSFL wants a single shared record of which seat is capable, it is asking for the opposite property.

mechanisms.name: EigenTrust (global reputation by distributed power iteration)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Normalises each peer's local trust ratings into a stochastic matrix and computes the principal eigenvector by distributed power iteration, giving every peer a single global trust value that is a transitive aggregate of the whole network's opinions.
mechanisms.citation: Sepandar D. Kamvar, Mario T. Schlosser, Hector Garcia-Molina, "The EigenTrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks", WWW 2003, pp. 640-651, DOI 10.1145/775152.775242.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It does NOT solve cold start without a prior. The algorithm requires a set of pre-trusted peers to anchor the eigenvector and to break ties when the trust graph is disconnected or when a newcomer has no incoming edges. A newcomer with no ratings has no well-defined position. Later critiques note high-reputation peers cluster around the pre-trusted set.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Trust is a unitless scalar, so heterogeneity is not represented at all. A fast malicious peer and a slow honest one are placed on the same axis.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Does not transfer, and the reason is the useful finding. EigenTrust is the canonical attempt to build the global, shared, auditable capability table CDSFL says it wants, in a P2P setting, and its load-bearing assumption is a set of pre-trusted peers chosen a priori. That is precisely 'routing by reputation rather than measurement' re-entering through the back door, and it violates the founder's first hard constraint. It also presumes transitive trust, which Andrade et al. deliberately reject because it reintroduces lying about third parties. Cite it to the founder as the proof that a global reputation number and a no-prior, no-names constraint are in tension.

mechanisms.name: Douceur's Sybil impossibility lemmas
mechanisms.what_it_does: Formally bounds what any identity-validation scheme can achieve without a logically central certifying authority. Lemma 1: if rho is the ratio of a faulty entity's resources to a minimally capable entity's, it can present g = rho distinct identities. Lemma 2: if a validator accepts identities that are not validated SIMULTANEOUSLY, one faulty entity can present an arbitrarily large number of identities, because the resources for each presentation are freed and reused. Lemma 3: if an identity is accepted when vouched for by q accepted identities, a faulty set F forges unboundedly many identities when |F| >= q or F's resources reach those of q + |F| minimal entities. Lemma 4: if validators do not coordinate their challenge intervals, even a minimally capable attacker presents floor(|C|/q) identities. Section 3.2 adds that computation challenges in particular can be BATCHED: given m puzzles y_1..y_m an entity can find a single witness satisfying all m at once.
mechanisms.citation: John R. Douceur, "The Sybil Attack", IPTPS 2002, Springer LNCS 2429, pp. 251-260, DOI 10.1007/3-540-45748-8_24. Conclusion: systems that do not establish distinct identities by an explicit or implicit certification authority "are susceptible to Sybil attacks".
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It says what cold-start capability measurement CANNOT do in a trustless setting: a resource challenge bounds identity count only if issued simultaneously to all claimants, by all validators concurrently, and only up to the resource ratio rho.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Heterogeneity is the attack budget. Section 3.1 states the premise explicitly: a resource-proof defence works only "if we assume that the resources of any two entities differ by at most a constant factor". CDSFL's hard constraint is that they differ by an unbounded factor.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the binding constraint on the whole dimension and it transfers in full. In a no-central-server CDSFL, nothing distinguishes 700 endpoints from 1 endpoint presenting 700 names, and the founder's own constraints make the bound worse rather than better. What breaks: either CDSFL keeps an identity authority for endpoints (the founder's own key store or a registry he signs), in which case it is not coordinator-free; or it accepts that the roster size is a claim, not a fact, and that measured capability can be concentrated in one operator presenting many names.

mechanisms.name: Crypto-puzzle node IDs and IP-derived IDs (S/Kademlia, BitTorrent BEP 42)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Makes identities costly rather than free. S/Kademlia requires a node ID satisfying a hash work requirement, uses parallel lookups over multiple disjoint paths so one malicious node cannot misdirect more than one query, and adds a sibling broadcast for replicated storage. BEP 42 instead constrains the node ID to a function of the node's external IP address.
mechanisms.citation: Ingmar Baumgart, Sebastian Mies, "S/Kademlia: A Practicable Approach Towards Secure Key-Based Routing", P2P-NVE 2007 / IEEE ICPADS, DOI 10.1109/ICPADS.2007.4447808. BitTorrent BEP 42, "DHT Security Extension" (Draft, Standards Track, last modified 2015), bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0042.html.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A newcomer pays a one-off computational entry fee, which is Friedman and Resnick's entry-fee remedy in concrete form. It bounds, but does not prevent, identity inflation.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Badly, and both specs admit it. A work-based entry fee is cheapest for exactly the participant with the most compute, so the admission control is regressive against the small desktop the founder wants to include. BEP 42 states its own limitation plainly: an entity's control over the DHT key space grows LINEARLY with its control over the IP address space.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as a cautionary datum rather than a design. These are the two best-engineered deployed answers to Douceur, and the empirical record is that they were insufficient: real sybil attacks were found running in BitTorrent's mainline DHT over long periods (Liang Wang, Jussi Kangasharju, "Real-World Sybil Attacks in BitTorrent Mainline DHT", IEEE GLOBECOM 2012; same authors, "Measuring Large-Scale Distributed Systems: Case of BitTorrent Mainline DHT", IEEE P2P 2013, reporting 15 to 27 million nodes per day), an eclipse attack against S/Kademlia-style mitigations was demonstrated and assigned CVE-2020-10937, and BEP 42 compliance is not enforced on remote nodes. [VERIFY:current] current BEP 42 adoption rates and whether the CVE has been remediated across implementations.

mechanisms.name: Social-graph Sybil resistance (Whanau)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Builds DHT routing tables from random walks over a social graph, so that the number of Sybils is irrelevant and only the number of attack edges (honest-to-Sybil links) matters. Tolerates up to O(n / log n) attack edges with n well-connected honest nodes, O(sqrt(n) log n) routing entries per node, constant-time lookups, and layered identifiers against clustering attacks. Validated on LiveJournal, Flickr, YouTube and DBLP graphs and on PlanetLab.
mechanisms.citation: Christopher Lesniewski-Laas, M. Frans Kaashoek, "Whanau: A Sybil-proof Distributed Hash Table", USENIX NSDI 2010.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By importing a prior from outside the system, namely the social graph. There is no cold start because trust is inherited from pre-existing human relationships.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not addressed; the graph encodes who vouches for whom, not how fast anyone is.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Does not transfer. It is the strongest known Sybil-resistance result for an open DHT and it works by substituting a human social prior for measurement. CDSFL's roster is model endpoints with no social graph, and importing one would mean routing by who-vouches-for-whom, i.e. by reputation, which the founder forbids. Worth citing precisely because it shows how much the state of the art has to assume to get Sybil resistance at all.

mechanisms.name: Distributed hash tables (Chord, Kademlia) and BitTorrent's trackerless mode
mechanisms.what_it_does: Provide exactly one primitive: given a key, find the node responsible for it, in O(log n) hops with O(log n) routing state. Kademlia uses XOR distance, whose symmetry means a node receives queries from the same distribution of nodes as populate its routing table. BitTorrent's BEP 5 uses a Kademlia variant so that, in the spec's words, each peer becomes a tracker.
mechanisms.citation: Petar Maymounkov, David Mazieres, "Kademlia: A Peer-to-peer Information System Based on the XOR Metric", IPTPS 2002. Ion Stoica, Robert Morris, David Karger, M. Frans Kaashoek, Hari Balakrishnan, "Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications", ACM SIGCOMM 2001. BitTorrent BEP 5, "DHT Protocol", Loewenstern and Norberg, bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0005.html.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It does not. Every DHT needs bootstrap contacts from outside the DHT. BEP 5 is explicit: a newly installed client downloading a trackerless torrent has no nodes in its routing table and depends on contacts included in the torrent file.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not at all. Key-space position is assigned by hash and is independent of capacity, so a desktop and a supercomputer carry the same share of the index.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the discovery layer and nothing more. A DHT gives CDSFL rendezvous ('who holds finding F?') with no coordinator. It gives it NO authenticity (a value retrieved is not authenticated to its claimed author), NO ordering (no 'who found it first'), NO durability guarantee, and NO access control. BEP 5's own documented consequence is that private communities disable DHT discovery because the protocol lacks authentication and access control, so any peer can freely join a swarm. If CDSFL wants its registry findings signed and ordered, that must be built above the DHT, not got from it.

mechanisms.name: BitTorrent's out-of-band root of trust (the metainfo file)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Every piece of content in a torrent is verified against a SHA1 hash fixed in advance by the publisher. BEP 3: the info dictionary's "pieces" field is "a string whose length is a multiple of 20", subdivided into 20-byte strings, "each of which is the SHA1 hash of the piece at the corresponding index". The "announce" field is "the URL of the tracker".
mechanisms.citation: Bram Cohen, BEP 3, "The BitTorrent Protocol Specification", bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0003.html. Trackerless operation: BEP 5, as above.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By fiat. The correct answer is published before the swarm exists.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Irrelevant; verification cost is the same for every participant.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the most important correction to 'a bit like BitTorrent' in the whole dimension. BitTorrent removed the coordinator from PEER DISCOVERY (BEP 5) and never from the ROOT OF TRUST. Integrity is entirely inherited from a centrally authored metainfo file obtained out of band, and even in trackerless mode the infohash itself still arrives out of band. A falsification harness has no pre-published root: findings are created at runtime and nobody knows the right answer in advance. CDSFL is therefore in the strictly harder case, and the BitTorrent analogy supplies an incentive mechanism but no integrity mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Epidemic and gossip protocols, and gossip-based aggregation
mechanisms.what_it_does: Anti-entropy: each site periodically compares its whole database with a random peer; very reliable but slow and too expensive to run often. Rumour mongering: a site treats a new update as a hot rumour and pushes it to random peers until it meets too many who already know it; much faster but with non-zero probability of incomplete delivery, so the two are combined with anti-entropy as a backstop. Deletions need death certificates, because absence cannot propagate. Gossip aggregation extends push-pull gossip with an update function (average, max, min, count), giving every node global quantities with variance among estimates decaying exponentially.
mechanisms.citation: Alan Demers, Dan Greene, Carl Hauser, Wes Irish, John Larson, Scott Shenker, Howard Sturgis, Dan Swinehart, Doug Terry, "Epidemic Algorithms for Replicated Database Maintenance", ACM PODC 1987 (extended as Xerox PARC CSL-89-1). Mark Jelasity, Alberto Montresor, Ozalp Babaoglu, "Gossip-based Aggregation in Large Dynamic Networks", ACM TOCS 23(3):219-252, 2005, DOI 10.1145/1082469.1082470.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start mechanism, but gossip aggregation removes a reason to need one: a global ranking statistic (mean score, max score, roster count) can be computed without any coordinator and without any node holding the full roster.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Message cost per node per round is constant and independent of network size, so a desktop participates on the same terms as a large node. This is the one mechanism in this dimension that genuinely scales from 1 to 700 participants with no redesign.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the dissemination layer for the finding registry, with one hard caveat that is directly load-bearing. Gossip gives eventual convergence of an ADD-ONLY set cheaply and coordinator-free. It does NOT give deletion, retraction or ordering for free: Demers et al. needed death certificates precisely because a retraction must be propagated as a positive fact. CDSFL retracts findings (the failure-later-refutation protocol is in the project's own directives), so the registry is not purely grow-only and the 1987 death-certificate problem lands on it directly, including the question of when a certificate may be discarded.

mechanisms.name: Grow-only sets, CRDTs, and the CALM theorem
mechanisms.what_it_does: A state-based CRDT whose payload forms a join semilattice, whose updates only move upward, and whose merge computes the least upper bound, converges to the same value on all replicas with no coordination, no consensus and no rollback, regardless of message order, duplication or failures. The grow-only set (merge = union) is the simplest instance. CALM makes the general statement: the programs with consistent, coordination-free distributed implementations are EXACTLY those expressible in monotonic logic.
mechanisms.citation: Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguica, Carlos Baquero, Marek Zawirski, "Conflict-free Replicated Data Types", SSS 2011, Springer LNCS 6976, pp. 386-400 (also INRIA RR-7687). Joseph M. Hellerstein, Peter Alvaro, "Keeping CALM: When Distributed Consistency is Easy", arXiv 1901.01930 / CACM 2020. Formal proof: Tom J. Ameloot, Frank Neven, Jan Van den Bussche, "Relational transducers for declarative networking", JACM 2013, framework of relational transducer networks.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not applicable; this is a data-structure result, not an allocation mechanism.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Merge cost is proportional to state, not to participant count, so slow participants converge later but never incorrectly.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the positive answer to the founder's question about the registry, and it is sharp. An append-only finding registry whose only operation is 'add a signed finding' IS monotonic, so by CALM it admits a coordination-free implementation and needs no consensus, no leader and no blockchain. Replicate it by gossip and it converges. What breaks the moment CDSFL steps outside that: any query of the form 'is this finding still open', 'who found it first', 'has the gate passed', or 'is this the complete set' is NON-monotonic, because its answer can be invalidated by a later arrival. CALM's contrapositive says those queries cannot be answered consistently without coordination. CDSFL's gates and closure decisions are exactly such queries, so the registry can be coordinator-free while the DECISIONS taken on it cannot.

mechanisms.name: Fork consistency (SUNDR) and the detect-not-prevent boundary
mechanisms.what_it_does: Establishes what is achievable for a shared log on infrastructure nobody trusts. A malicious or buggy store can always present different clients with different, mutually consistent-looking views (a fork). It cannot be prevented. Fork consistency guarantees that all clients see an identical log up to the first concealed operation, that no client sees another's operations after it, and therefore that the fork is DETECTABLE as soon as the two clients compare views. Detection requires an out-of-band channel. The stronger property is fork-linearizability, and SUNDR's overhead grows with the number of clients.
mechanisms.citation: Jinyuan Li, Maxwell Krohn, David Mazieres, Dennis Shasha, "Secure Untrusted Data Repository (SUNDR)", USENIX OSDI 2004, pp. 121-136. Follow-up with O(n) per-operation overhead: Christian Cachin, Abhi Shelat, Alexander Shraer, on fork-linearizable storage.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not applicable.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not applicable.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the exact theory for 'a shared append-only finding registry maintained without a coordinator'. The answer the literature gives is: you get DETECTION, not PREVENTION, and only if participants actually compare views out of band. For an auditable falsification record that is a real but limited guarantee: a seat cannot rewrite history undetectably, but it CAN be shown a registry in which an inconvenient finding never existed, and nothing inside the protocol will tell it so. What breaks if adopted: the project must accept that 'the record is complete' is not a property the registry can assert, only a property an auditor can retrospectively confirm by comparing two views, and must build the comparison channel, which is the step that fails in practice (see Certificate Transparency below).

mechanisms.name: Certificate Transparency: the deployed-world evidence on coordinator-free append-only logs
mechanisms.what_it_does: The largest production append-only Merkle log in existence. RFC 9162 section 1: "The append-only property of each log is achieved using Merkle Trees"; section 4: "A log is a single, append-only Merkle Tree of submitted certificate and precertificate entries." And then, in the same section 1, the concession: the auditing mechanisms "can be circumvented by a misbehaving log that shows different, inconsistent views of itself to different clients", therefore "it is necessary to treat each log as a trusted third party", and stronger mechanisms "are outside the scope of this document". The gossip layer meant to close that gap proposed SCT Feedback, STH Pollination and a Trusted Auditor Relationship, and would force a log to produce a consistency proof between conflicting tree heads, which a forked log cannot do.
mechanisms.citation: RFC 9162, "Certificate Transparency Version 2.0", December 2021 (Experimental; obsoletes RFC 6962), sections 1 and 4. Linus Nordberg, Daniel Kahn Gillmor, Tom Ritter, draft-ietf-trans-gossip-05, "Gossiping in CT", January 2018, expired July 2018, never published as an RFC. Rasmus Dahlberg et al., "Aggregation-Based Certificate Transparency Gossip", arXiv 1806.08817 / SECURWARE 2019: "despite CT being adopted by several major browser vendors, no gossip mechanism is widely deployed".
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not applicable.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not applicable.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the strongest empirical answer to the founder's core question, and it is a negative one. An append-only auditable log, backed by every major browser vendor, specified over more than a decade, with enormous commercial incentive, STILL designates each log a trusted third party and still has no widely deployed mechanism for coordinator-free split-view detection. If that effort has not shipped the gossip layer, a research harness should not plan on building one. The actionable transfer: CT's working substitute is third-party AUDITORS and bulletin-board designs, i.e. a small number of independent witnesses rather than full peer-to-peer gossip. That is the realistic target for CDSFL. [VERIFY:current] whether any CT gossip mechanism has reached wide deployment since 2021.

mechanisms.name: PeerReview (accountability via tamper-evident logs and witnesses)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each node keeps a secure, signed, hash-chained record of every message it sent and received. Each node is audited by witnesses who replay its log against a reference implementation. Guarantees that any Byzantine fault whose effects are observed by a correct node is eventually detected and irrefutably linked to a faulty node, and that a correct node can always defend itself against a false accusation. Assumes correct nodes are deterministic, nodes can sign messages, and each node is periodically checked by a correct node. Evaluated on a network filesystem, a P2P system and an overlay multicast system.
mechanisms.citation: Andreas Haeberlen, Petr Kouznetsov, Peter Druschel, "PeerReview: Practical Accountability for Distributed Systems", ACM SOSP 2007, pp. 175-188 (also MPI-SWS-2007-003). Later critique on the eventual-delivery assumption: Zhifeng Xiao, Yang Xiao, "PeerReview re-evaluation for accountability in distributed systems or networks", 2012.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a ranking mechanism, but it supplies the primitive a measured-capability system needs: an unforgeable, attributable record of what each participant actually did, with no coordinator holding it.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Audit cost falls on the witnesses, so a small peer witnessing a large one bears cost proportional to the large peer's traffic. That is a real asymmetry against the desktop participant.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the best fit in the literature for 'auditable record among untrusted peers without a coordinator', and it is the design CDSFL should study first. The witness set is a small committee rather than the whole network, which is the same compromise CT reached in practice. What breaks on adoption: PeerReview requires DETERMINISM of correct nodes to replay logs against a reference implementation. Language-model seats are not deterministic, so the replay check cannot be applied to a seat's reasoning. It CAN be applied to the harness's own code paths and to the tool invocations a seat made, which is where CDSFL's past defects have actually lived.

mechanisms.name: Result verification by spot-checking (ringers) and by replication (BOINC)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Ringers: the task issuer plants inputs whose answers it already knows into the work unit, so a returned result can be checked cheaply without redoing the work, making cheating unprofitable; stronger variants let a participant prove it did most of the assigned work with high probability, at very little overhead. The technique is restricted to inversion of a one-way function. Replication: each job runs on 2 unrelated hosts, and if outputs agree within an application-specific validator's tolerance they are accepted, otherwise a third instance is issued until a quorum or an instance limit is reached, with homogeneous redundancy to cope with floating-point divergence. Adaptive replication tracks consecutive validated jobs per (host, application version) pair and makes replication probabilistic, with probability falling toward 0 as the streak grows.
mechanisms.citation: Philippe Golle, Ilya Mironov, "Uncheatable Distributed Computations", CT-RSA 2001, Springer LNCS 2020, pp. 425-440. Extension beyond one-way-function inversion: Doug Szajda, Barry Lawson, Jason Owen, IEEE Security and Privacy 2003. Replication and adaptive replication: David P. Anderson, "BOINC: A Platform for Volunteer Computing", arXiv 1903.01699 / Journal of Grid Computing 2020. NOTE: the task brief says "Golle-Mitchell"; the spot-checking paper is Golle and MIRONOV. There is a separate Golle and Stubblebine paper on secure distributed computing in a commercial environment. Worth correcting before the citation is reused.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Adaptive replication IS a cold-start-to-trusted ramp: a new host is fully replicated, and replication decays as its validated streak grows. This is the measured-capability ladder the founder wants, already built, already deployed, and tracked per (host, application version) rather than per host, because a machine may be reliable on one workload and not another.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Explicitly, via homogeneous redundancy: further instances of a numerically unstable job go only to machines in the same equivalence class as the first. Cross-class results are not compared at all, which is the formal version of 'do not pitch a desktop against a supercomputer'.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers well and should be the default. Plain 2-way replication costs at least half of effective capacity; adaptive replication is reported to move that factor close to 1 while keeping a low error-rate bound even with malicious volunteers. Per-(seat, task-class) reliability tracking is directly applicable to CDSFL's seats. The ringer technique does NOT transfer directly, because it needs a planted input whose answer the issuer knows, and the whole point of a falsification task is that nobody knows the answer. Its CDSFL analogue is a seeded known-defect injected into a target article, which the project can construct. [VERIFY:current] exact BOINC adaptive-replication thresholds and formula, which are in the server source rather than the published docs.

mechanisms.name: Refereed delegation of computation (bisection on disagreement)
mechanisms.what_it_does: A weak verifier obtains the correct answer from k servers provided AT LEAST 1 is honest, without trusting any of them and without doing the work itself. If two servers return the same answer it is correct by assumption. If they disagree, the verifier runs a binary search over the computation trace: each side reports the configuration at the midpoint between a known-good and known-bad step, narrowing until a single step is isolated, at which point the cheater is identified. Soundness holds even if the malicious servers communicate during the protocol, and the referee learns WHICH server cheated. Logarithmically many rounds for any efficiently computable function under collision-resistant hashing.
mechanisms.citation: Ran Canetti, Ben Riva, Guy N. Rothblum, "Refereed Delegation of Computation", Information and Computation 226:16-36, 2013 (earlier version IACR ePrint 2011/518, "Two 1-Round Protocols for Delegation of Computation"). Predecessor: Uriel Feige, Joe Kilian, refereed games.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It makes cold start partly unnecessary: with no prior whatsoever, 2 untrusted participants and a cheap referee yield a correct answer AND an attribution of blame. The attribution accumulates into exactly the measured capability record the founder wants, generated as a by-product of doing real work rather than by a separate startup tournament.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The referee's work is logarithmic in the computation length and independent of the servers' capacity, so the arbiter can be the smallest participant in the system. This is the cleanest fit to the heterogeneity constraint in this whole dimension.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Strongest genuinely novel-adjacent transfer available. CDSFL's seats already disagree, and the project's existing record shows cases where neither seat's fix dominated. Bisecting a disagreement until a single checkable step is isolated is a better primitive than voting, which the project has independently banned. What breaks: the protocol requires a DETERMINISTIC, step-addressable computation trace. A model's reasoning is neither. It applies to the derivation a seat emits (a proof, a script, a falsifier) and not to how the seat arrived at it, so CDSFL would need to require that every claim ship with a replayable artifact. That is a tightening of the project's existing measured-rate-travels-with-its-script rule, not a new concept.

mechanisms.name: BAR fault tolerance (Byzantine, Altruistic, Rational) and the cost of a coordinator-free shared log
mechanisms.what_it_does: Models cooperative services spanning multiple administrative domains where nodes may be Byzantine (broken, misconfigured, malicious) OR rational (deviating selfishly for local benefit), and builds a three-level architecture plus BAR-B, a backup service tolerating Byzantine users and an unbounded number of rational ones, on an asynchronous replicated state machine. The technical report states the bound as at most (n-2)/3 Byzantine nodes, with the rest permitted to be rational.
mechanisms.citation: Amitanand S. Aiyer, Lorenzo Alvisi, Allen Clement, Mike Dahlin, Jean-Philippe Martin, Carl Porth, "BAR Fault Tolerance for Cooperative Services", ACM SOSP 2005, DOI 10.1145/1095810.1095816 (extended as UT-Austin TR-05-10). Measured: the BAR-tolerant state machine executes 15 requests per second; BAR-B backs up 100 MB in under 4 minutes. The TR variant reports 20 requests per second and 1 GB in 20 minutes. Underlying Byzantine bound: Marshall Pease, Robert Shostak, Leslie Lamport, "Reaching Agreement in the Presence of Faults", JACM 27(2):228-234, 1980. Asynchronous impossibility: Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch, Michael Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process", JACM 32(2):374-382, 1985.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not applicable.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Poorly: a replicated state machine requires every replica to execute every request, so the slowest replica caps throughput and the desktop participant becomes the bottleneck.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Cite it for the price tag. This is the honest, rigorous, no-trusted-coordinator answer to 'a totally ordered shared record among untrusted, self-interested peers', and it costs 15 requests per second, requires more than 3 times the number of Byzantine faults to be tolerated in replicas, and cannot terminate deterministically under full asynchrony (FLP). CDSFL's registry would be writing tens of findings per experiment, so the throughput is survivable, but the replica-count and determinism requirements are not free. The right conclusion is the one the CRDT/CALM result gives: do not pay for total order on a structure that only needs union.

mechanisms.name: Blockchain consensus as the wrong tool
mechanisms.what_it_does: Supplies a decision procedure for when a blockchain is warranted. A blockchain is indicated only when state must be stored, there are MULTIPLE writers, an always-online trusted third party is NOT usable, and the writers do not trust each other; permissionless specifically only when the writers are also UNKNOWN.
mechanisms.citation: Karl Wust, Arthur Gervais, "Do you need a Blockchain?", IEEE Crypto Valley Conference on Blockchain Technology (CVCBT) 2018, pp. 45-54, DOI 10.1109/CVCBT.2018.00011 (IACR ePrint 2017/375).
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Proof-of-work bounds identity creation by resource expenditure, which is Douceur's resource challenge with global simultaneity provided by the chain. It is the only mechanism here that actually satisfies Douceur's Lemma 2, and it costs a global energy market to do so.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Adversely. Influence is proportional to resources by design, which is the exact opposite of the founder's requirement that a desktop not be pitched against a supercomputer.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Does not transfer, and the decision procedure says so on its own terms. CDSFL's writers are KNOWN (they are endpoints the founder configures) and an always-online trusted party IS available (the founder himself, as the human in the loop, by the project's own design). Both conditions independently route to 'use a database'. Beyond that, the blockchain mechanism would actively violate two hard constraints: it allocates influence by resource share, and it makes identity cost money, which penalises the small participant the founder wants included. The append-only property CDSFL actually wants is supplied by hash-chaining and Merkle trees, which predate and are independent of consensus; total ordering is the part that costs, and the CALM result says a grow-only registry does not need it.

mechanisms.name: Whitewashing, cheap pseudonyms, and the necessity of distrusting newcomers
mechanisms.what_it_does: Proves that when identities are free, no equilibrium sustains significantly more cooperation than a dues-paying equilibrium in which newcomers are treated poorly until they earn standing. The inefficiency is not a design flaw to be engineered away; it is the price of optional reputation. Remedies considered: disallowing anonymity (impractical), entry fees (exclude low-payoff but legitimate participants), and unchangeable pseudonyms via blind signatures and a third party. Follow-on work quantifies the social cost and finds that blanket newcomer penalties raise social cost only in limited and rare scenarios and at high churn rates. Empirically, free riding at scale: almost 70% of observed users shared no files, and the top 1% of sharing hosts returned nearly 50% of all responses.
mechanisms.citation: Eric J. Friedman, Paul Resnick, "The Social Cost of Cheap Pseudonyms", Journal of Economics and Management Strategy 10(2):173-199, 2001. Michal Feldman, Christos Papadimitriou, John Chuang, Ion Stoica, "Free-riding and Whitewashing in Peer-to-Peer Systems", IEEE JSAC 24(5):1010-1019, 2006 (earlier at WEIS 2004 and the SIGCOMM 2004 PINS workshop). Eytan Adar, Bernardo A. Huberman, "Free Riding on Gnutella", First Monday 5(10), 2000, DOI 10.5210/fm.v5i10.792.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It constrains it. A cold-start mechanism that gives a newcomer the SAME expected allocation as a proven contributor is provably exploitable when identities are free, because the cheapest way to look like a newcomer is to become one. Any coordinator-free CDSFL must therefore give newcomers a bounded, discounted allocation, which is exactly what optimistic unchoking (1 of 4 slots) and OurGrid (reputation exactly 0, floored, with a sublinear history bonus) both do.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The entry-fee remedy is explicitly regressive: it excludes participants with low payoffs, which is the small participant.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is where the founder's hard constraint collides with a theorem. 'No model is ever permanently set aside; a bad performer is reassigned, not deleted' is compatible with the literature. 'A reassigned model gets the same shot as a proven one' is not. OurGrid's max{0, ...} formulation is the published reconciliation: the floor at 0 means nobody is ever worse off than a newcomer (never set aside), and the sublinear history term means veterans never become unovertakeable (always reachable), while the fact that reputation CANNOT go below 0 is precisely what makes resetting identity worthless.

mechanisms.name: Secure Scuttlebutt (per-author append-only logs, subjective replication)
mechanisms.what_it_does: A shipped peer-to-peer protocol with no central authority whose single source of truth is per-identity cryptographically secured append-only logs. Each event is named by author identity plus sequence number, messages are SHA256-hashed and Ed25519-signed, and replication follows the social graph so a participant downloads only the feeds it follows. Works over the Internet, local networks and sneakernets. Explicitly embraces a SUBJECTIVE reader model: there is no single global view, only each reader's partial one.
mechanisms.citation: Dominic Tarr, Erick Lavoie, Aljoscha Meyer, Christian Tschudin, "Secure Scuttlebutt: An Identity-Centric Protocol for Subjective and Decentralized Applications", ACM ICN 2019, DOI 10.1145/3357150.3357396. Follow-up: Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Erick Lavoie, Christian Tschudin, "Gossiping with Append-Only Logs in Secure-Scuttlebutt", ACM ICN 2020.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: The paper names the onboarding problem as an explicit open topic; a new identity has no followers and is therefore invisible until somebody follows it, which is a social act outside the protocol.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Well. Per-author logs mean each participant stores only what it chose to follow, so a small participant carries a small subset and is still a full peer.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the concrete architecture to copy for the registry, and it sidesteps the hardest problem by changing the data model. Instead of ONE shared append-only registry needing agreement on its contents, give each seat its own signed, hash-chained, append-only log and define the registry as the union of the logs a reader has replicated. That union is a grow-only set, so by CALM it converges coordinator-free; each entry is attributable and tamper-evident by signature and sequence number; and forks within one author's log are detectable because two different messages at the same sequence number are self-evident proof of misbehaviour. What breaks, and the founder must decide whether he accepts it: the record becomes SUBJECTIVE. There is no moment at which the registry is complete, and two auditors may hold different unions. For a falsification harness whose whole point is an auditable record, that is a substantive loss, and it is the unavoidable price of removing the coordinator.

strongest_disagreement:
The literature contradicts the cold-start maths-problem mechanism specifically in the no-central-server setting, and it does so with a formal result, not a judgement.

A hard randomly generated maths problem issued to every participant at startup is, in Douceur's taxonomy, a COMPUTATION RESOURCE CHALLENGE. Three of his four lemmas apply to it directly (Douceur, "The Sybil Attack", IPTPS 2002, LNCS 2429, pp. 251-260).

Lemma 1 sets the attack budget: "If rho is the ratio of the resources of a faulty entity f to the resources of a minimally capable entity, then f can present g = rho distinct identities to local entity l." The founder's heterogeneity constraint says a desktop PC and a vast supercomputer stack must both be admissible participants. That constraint IS the statement that rho is large. Whoever owns the largest machine can therefore present rho names, enter the tournament rho times, and win rho top-tier slots legitimately on measured performance. The two hard constraints "capability is a measured quantity, never a name" and "heterogeneous participants" are not independent: jointly, in a trustless setting, they maximise the Sybil surface, because they remove the only cheap identity anchor (the name) while widening the resource ratio that bounds forgery.

Lemma 2 is worse for a STARTUP tournament specifically: "If local entity l accepts entities that are not validated simultaneously, then a single faulty entity f can present an arbitrarily large number of distinct identities to entity l", because "the resources required for each presentation are used and then freed for the subsequent presentation." A recursive ladder that assesses the top performers, then issues a less complex problem to the remainder, then recurses, is BY CONSTRUCTION non-simultaneous. One endpoint can win tier 1, then re-enter the tier 2 round under a second name using the same hardware.

And Douceur's section 3.2 closes the obvious patch. Computation challenges, uniquely among the three resource types he considers, can be BATCHED: "it is possible for an entity to solve multiple puzzles simultaneously by combining them. If an entity receives m puzzles y_1, y_2, ... y_m, it can find a w such that..." (he contrasts this with storage challenges, where he gives an information-theoretic argument that batching is impossible, since every bit stored for one challenger is unavailable to another). So even enforcing simultaneity does not save a maths-problem challenge: a single endpoint can answer all m concurrent challenges as m apparent participants.

The knockout bracket fares no better on this axis, and arguably worse. A bracket is a global, stateful, round-structured object: somebody must hold the bracket, decide the pairings, and declare the winners. That somebody is a coordinator, which is the thing the design is trying to eliminate. A bracket is also the most Sybil-amplifying tournament shape there is: padding the field with g = rho identities under Lemma 1 lets one operator guarantee itself a semi-final slot by arranging to meet only itself, and because the bracket assumes NO capability at the outset there is no prior against which that anomaly can be flagged.

The second, independent contradiction is with the constraint that no model is ever permanently set aside. Friedman and Resnick prove that with free identities, no equilibrium sustains significantly more cooperation than a dues-paying equilibrium in which newcomers are treated poorly until they earn standing ("The Social Cost of Cheap Pseudonyms", Journal of Economics and Management Strategy 10(2):173-199, 2001). If a badly performing model is reassigned to the same expected allocation a newcomer receives, then the optimal strategy for a bad performer is to present as a newcomer, and the project's own constraint supplies the escape hatch. The reconciliation already exists and is precise: OurGrid's r_A(B) = max{0, v(B,A) - v(A,B) + sqrt(v(B,A))} (Andrade, Brasileiro, Cirne, Mowbray, HPDC 2004, section 3.1, eq. 4). Floor at 0 so nobody is ever ranked below a newcomer, which is "never permanently set aside" AND is what makes identity-resetting worthless; sublinear history term so veterans never become unovertakeable.

Finally, on the registry: the founder should be told that the auditability goal and the no-coordinator goal are in direct tension, with a production-scale datum behind it. RFC 9162 section 1 states that Certificate Transparency's auditing mechanisms "can be circumvented by a misbehaving log that shows different, inconsistent views of itself to different clients", concludes "it is necessary to treat each log as a trusted third party", and places stronger mechanisms out of scope. The gossip protocol designed to fix exactly that (draft-ietf-trans-gossip-05, expired July 2018, never an RFC) is still not widely deployed. A falsification harness whose core data structure is an auditable append-only registry should not expect to solve, as a side project, the problem that the global certificate ecosystem has left open for over a decade.
open_problems: Coordinator-free split-view detection for an append-only log is unsolved IN PRACTICE, not just in CDSFL. The theory (fork consistency, SUNDR, OSDI 2004) says detection is achievable and prevention is not; the deployment record (RFC 9162 section 1, and draft-ietf-trans-gossip-05 expiring unpublished in 2018) says even detection has not shipped at scale. Nobody has a working answer to give CDSFL.

Sybil resistance without either a central certifying authority, a resource-parity assumption, or an imported social graph. Douceur 2002 showed the first two are required; Whanau (NSDI 2010) achieves it only with the third. CDSFL has none of the three: no authority if it is coordinator-free, unbounded resource disparity by explicit constraint, and no social graph among model endpoints.

Verification of a NON-DETERMINISTIC worker's output. Every result-verification mechanism in this literature assumes the work is reproducible: BOINC's replication needs two hosts to agree within a tolerance, PeerReview needs correct nodes to be deterministic so logs can be replayed against a reference implementation, and refereed delegation needs a step-addressable trace to bisect. Language-model seats satisfy none of these. The partial workaround is to verify the ARTIFACT a seat emits rather than the seat, which narrows the guarantee to 'the proof checks' and never reaches 'the seat is competent'.

Capability measurement where the task has no known answer. Golle and Mironov's ringers need a planted input whose answer the issuer knows, and the technique is anyway restricted to inversion of a one-way function. A genuine falsification target has no planted answer. Seeded known-defect injection is the obvious substitute but it measures the ability to find PLANTED defects, which is a different quantity from the ability to find real ones, and nothing in this literature bounds the gap.

Non-monotonic queries over a coordination-free registry. CALM (Hellerstein and Alvaro, arXiv 1901.01930; proved by Ameloot et al., JACM 2013) says a grow-only registry needs no coordination, and says equally that any query whose answer a later arrival can invalidate does. 'Is this finding still open', 'has the gate passed', 'is the set complete' and 'who found it first' are all in the second class. There is no known way to answer them coordination-free, and CDSFL's gates are exactly these questions.

Retraction in a gossip-replicated registry. Demers et al. (PODC 1987) needed death certificates because absence does not propagate, and when a death certificate may safely be discarded is still a design-by-judgement problem. CDSFL retracts findings under its own failure-later-refutation protocol, so a purely grow-only registry is not what it actually needs.

The cost curve of coordinator-free total order is known and bad, but not improved. BAR-B (SOSP 2005) reached 15 requests per second with a bound of at most (n-2)/3 Byzantine replicas, and FLP (JACM 1985) rules out deterministic termination under full asynchrony. No cheaper construction has displaced this for the Byzantine-plus-rational setting.

Whether capability-by-measurement and whitewash resistance can be reconciled WITHOUT a reputation floor. OurGrid's max{0,...} is the only published construction that gets both, and it buys them by making reputation deliberately subjective and non-transitive, which means no global capability table exists. Whether a global, auditable capability ranking can coexist with 'never set anyone aside' and free identities is, on the Friedman-Resnick result, probably no, but it has not been settled as a theorem for this specific setting.
